title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Introduction
text: Memorilla is a new memory system for LLMs from Adibvafa Fallahpour, Parsa Idehpour, Vignesh Kothapalli, Nikita Mounier, Shirley Wu, Shayan Pardis, and Jure Leskovec. Rather than pasting retrieved text into the prompt, it reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM a fixed set of 16 learned input embeddings. The code, weights, and data are all open today, with a released module for Qwen3-8B. We are not part of the Memorilla team. This post is our independent early look at the release, and "we" below refers to our own reading and our own reproduction work. Here are a few highlights: - Fixed token budget: The LLM receives 16 soft tokens however large the collection grows. On NarrativeQA that means 16 document tokens per query against 67,385 for full context, or 4,212x fewer. On FactKG it means 108x fewer. - Collection-wide reads: There is no top-k cutoff. Each query attends over every stored document embedding, so evidence that looks nothing like the question can still reach the model. - Reusable store: Each document is encoded once with a frozen encoder. A new user needs no retraining, so one module serves every user of the same LLM. - Trained through a frozen LLM: The m

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: What Memorilla changes for LLM memory
text: Figure 1. Document tokens each method gives the LLM per query on NarrativeQA. Chart by AIYatra, data from Table 10 of the Memorilla paper Once training ends, an LLM only knows what fits in its context window. Full context pastes everything in, which raises inference cost and can also hurt quality as the prompt grows ( Lost in the Middle , Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance ). Retrieval keeps the prompt small, but it only surfaces chunks that resemble the question. Memory layers such as Mem0 and MemGPT organize stored information much better, though they still select some text and place it in the prompt. Memorilla replaces that selection step with a small trained network. Take the example in the project's README. A user with 107 past conversations, about 32,000 tokens in total, asks for easy breakfast ideas that keep them full all morning. A frozen Qwen3-8B then opens its answer with: Since you've got a family history of type 2 diabetes, you might enjoy breakfasts that balance protein, healthy fats, and fiber to keep you full without spiking blood sugar... The user never stated that history. The only clue is one old chat asking whether diabetes on the mother's side raises a

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: The Memorilla architecture
text: Figure 2. Overview of the Memorilla architecture. Snowflakes mark frozen components and the flame marks the trained one. Source: Fallahpour et al., Memorilla repository, assets/architecture.png, Apache 2.0. Memorilla delivers its fixed budget by separating storage, recall, and generation into three components, and only the middle one is trained. Store. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder turns each chunk into one mean-pooled vector of 2,560 values. A 200-chat history becomes a 200 x 2,560 matrix of about 1 MB. This is the same work a dense retrieval index already does, so the write path adds no extra cost over RAG. Recall. Sixteen learned slots first cross-attend to the question, then pass through two blocks of cross-attention and feed-forward layers that read all N documents, following the latent-array design of Perceiver. Notably, every document gets some attention weight, however small. Generation. A linear layer projects each slot from 2,560 to the 4,096 dimensions of Qwen3-8B, and the results overwrite 16 placeholder embeddings in the prompt. title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Memorilla release status
text: The Memorilla release covers the training pipeline, the evaluation pipeline, checkpoints for each training stage, and a new benchmark. In this section, we highlight the query-conditioned read that drives the results, then the usability of the release and its training recipes.

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Query-conditioned soft tokens
text: Figure 3. One Memorilla read in tensor shapes for the Qwen3-8B setup. Diagram by AIYatra, based on Section 2 of the Memorilla paper and memorilla/memory.py The central design choice is that the slots read the question before they read the documents, as shown in Figure 3. The 16 learned slots are shared across all users and queries. A cross-attention step conditions them on the question embedding, and the conditioned slots then read the store, so the same store can answer different questions with different memory tokens. Since the module adds no positional encoding, the read treats the store as an unordered set. Figure 4. Slot construction ablation on PersonaMem-v2, higher is better. Chart by AIYatra, data from Table 13 of the Memorilla paper Figure 4 compares seven ways of building the 16 slots with one training recipe. Parameters alone do not close the gap: a documents-only variant with 269M parameters reaches 34.72. Hard selection lags as well, with the 16 most similar documents and a full parameter budget reaching 33.86. Query conditioning with soft attention reaches 44.04, and Memorilla achieves this while dropping the self-attention of a BLIP-2-style Q-Former, saving 79M param

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Out-of-the-box usability
text: The release is straightforward to try on suitable hardware. The quickstart needs Linux, CUDA, Python 3.11, and one 80 GB GPU, and it downloads about 25 GB of models. We list the commands in the appendix. Weights and data. memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B hosts the checkpoints for Stages 1, 2, and 3, plus specializations for PersonalizationV4 and PersonaMem-v2. memorilla/Memorilla-Data provides training and evaluation data with precomputed embeddings. The code is Apache 2.0. A new benchmark. memorilla/PersonalizationV4 has 149 synthetic users with 200 chats each, where every question requires combining at least two facts. It is released under CC BY 4.0. Model coverage. Every supervised experiment pairs Qwen with Qwen, and a new LLM needs a new module. Because memory enters through input embeddings, Memorilla requires open weights and your own serving stack, so hosted text APIs are out of scope for now.

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Three-stage training
text: Figure 5. The Memorilla training curriculum. Diagram by AIYatra, based on Section 2.6 and Tables 1, 4, and 5 of the Memorilla paper Stage 1 teaches preservation: with 1.98M Wikipedia passages, the LLM must write a paraphrase from memory alone. Stage 2 teaches selective recall across 1.34M examples from ten sources, including SQuAD, DROP, MS MARCO, and CNN/DailyMail. Stage 3 fine-tunes a single checkpoint on the training splits of all eight benchmarks, with five more epochs each for PersonaMem-v2 and PersonalizationV4. The README puts the three stages at about 19 hours on four H100 80 GB GPUs, with about 310 GiB of data and embeddings to download.

title: Memorilla for Frozen LLMs: 16 Memory Tokens and 4,212x Fewer Tokens than Full Context
heading: Next Steps
text: Sixteen tokens on one model family is a strong first result, and the most interesting work is still ahead. The authors point to hybrid memory and retrieval, encoders trained for compression, transfer across model families, multimodal stores, and one store serving multiple LLMs. On FactKG, 15.9% of questions are answered by Memorilla alone and 10.0% by RAG-50 alone, so the hybrid direction looks especially promising. From our side, we would most like to see the community: - Run RAG on a task-tuned decoder against Memorilla. - Give each PersonaMem-v2 question another user's store, to isolate what personal memory contributes. - Evaluate Memorilla on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and a test built around changing facts. - Extend quality and latency measurements beyond N=512. - Test abstention, since a fixed token budget gives the model no signal that information is missing. - Study memory poisoning, since attacker text in the store influences vectors that are harder to audit than retrieved text. - Keep vLLM patched and compute memory tokens server-side. Public endpoints should never accept raw embeddings from clients, and vLLM's prompt-embedding path had CVE-2025-62164.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Introduction
text: A cactus is approaching. The dinosaur has three choices: keep running, jump, or duck. Make the wrong choice at the wrong moment and the run ends. Tiny Dino, a project published by GitHub user syedazeez337, turns that familiar game into a compact machine-learning experiment. Its shipped policy has just 21,699 parameters . The repository reports that this checkpoint completed 1,000,000 simulated frames without a crash , with no runtime planner correcting its actions. The useful story is how the project connects a small model to a precise input contract, an offline teacher, and several checks on the exact artifact being deployed. Reading the code also reveals boundaries that matter when interpreting those results.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: What the network actually sees
text: This policy does not watch screenshots. It receives a 28-value structured state vector extracted directly from the simulation. Those features describe the game speed, the dinosaur’s vertical position and velocity, its movement and control state, and the two nearest obstacles. Obstacle features include relative distance, width, height, vertical position, and type. Missing-obstacle indicators distinguish an absent obstacle from an obstacle whose numeric features happen to be zero. The distinction matters. Recognizing a cactus in an image and choosing when to jump are separate problems. Tiny Dino focuses on choosing actions once the relevant state is available. Its engine advances at a fixed 60 frames per second and reimplements Chromium-related physics and collision semantics. Courses are seeded, making runs repeatable within this implementation. This is a controlled simulator rather than a screen-reading agent operating an arbitrary browser game.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: A small network with a clear job
text: Architecture at a glance. The teacher supplies supervision offline; the deployed policy chooses each action directly. Diagram based on the repository implementation. The deployed architecture is a feed-forward multilayer perceptron with three hidden layers, each 96 units wide, SiLU activations, and three output scores. Its dimensions are: 28 inputs → 96 → 96 → 96 → 3 action scores Including biases, that is 21,699 trainable parameters. The shipped FP32 checkpoint occupies 90,929 bytes; that file includes metadata as well as weights. At each frame, the runtime extracts and normalizes the state, runs the network, computes action probabilities, and selects the largest probability. It applies that action directly to the engine. There is no teacher consulted during live play and no fallback rule that replaces a risky prediction. The runtime validates inputs, output shape, and finite values, but those checks do not choose a safer action. The model remains responsible for the gameplay decision. The probability display in the web app helps readers inspect the model’s preferences. It should not be interpreted as a calibrated probability of surviving the next obstacle.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: A timing intuition
text: Imagine the same cactus at the same distance in two runs, with the game moving faster in the second. The dinosaur has less time to react in that faster run. If it is already falling from a jump, the useful action may change again. That is why the inputs include speed and motion, as well as obstacle distance.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: An offline teacher supplies the examples
text: A tiny policy can be cheap at inference because more work happens before deployment. Tiny Dino’s teacher evaluates the three candidate first actions by forward simulation. After that first step it follows a deterministic continuation policy, looking ahead for a bounded number of frames or until the target obstacle is passed. Certification uses a 90-frame horizon. This is narrower than searching every possible future action sequence. A teacher-approved action survives the particular bounded rollout used by the checker; it is not a guarantee of indefinite survival. The corpus generator uses these verdicts to choose labels. It prefers the teacher’s continuation action when acceptable and otherwise picks an acceptable alternative. The training command also adds offline expert trajectories from a separate seed group and repeats boundary examples to emphasize timing-sensitive cases. The repository contains a DAgger-style collector for states visited by a learned policy. However, the exposed training command currently adds teacher-controlled expert rollouts. These are distinct data-collection paths, and the code does not establish that the shipped checkpoint came from a full iterative DAg

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: What the recorded results show
text: Different checks answer different questions. These figures summarize committed repository records, not a fresh benchmark. The following numbers come from the repository’s committed evidence and deployment records. They are reported results, not measurements independently rerun for this article. Check Recorded result Deployed model 21,699 parameters, FP32 Checkpoint file 90,929 bytes Frozen certification grid 5,400 states checked Choices rejected by the bounded teacher 0 Certification cases excluded for no acceptable action 0 Held-out and soak evaluation 20 seeds, 50,000 frames each Total simulated frames 1,000,000 Recorded crashes 0 Runtime action interventions 0 Reported CPU latency 0.0484 ms p50; 0.0545 ms p95; 0.0709 ms p99 The certification grid varies speeds, obstacle distances, obstacle types and bird heights, control ages, and selected paired-obstacle gaps. It deliberately samples distances densely around timing boundaries. Those latency figures should stay attached to their recorded benchmark. They do not measure browser rendering, HTTP round trips, or an end-to-end user interaction, and they are not a promise for every machine.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Why certification and long runs answer different questions
text: The certification checker asks whether each selected action belongs to the teacher’s acceptable set on a fixed grid. Long runs ask whether sequences of the model’s own decisions keep the game alive. There is an additional detail in the implementation: the corpus generator uses the same synthetic scenario grid as certification. Changing the seed field does not turn these synthetic states into unseen feature combinations. Passing this grid is therefore a finite conformance check, not an independent held-out generalization benchmark. The trajectory tests provide complementary evidence, but they also remain finite: seeds 201 through 220, with a fixed maximum length per run. They do not cover every possible course, state, physics variation, or future frame. The project records a useful failure. A GPU-trained candidate passed certification but failed its soak evaluation, so it was rejected. The README also describes a retrained model crashing on seed 202 at frame 2,327 after passing certification. That is why a successful retraining run cannot simply inherit the shipped model’s results. The new weights need their own checks.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Two optimizations that did not earn deployment
text: The repository’s INT8 experiment reduced the candidate artifact to 29,049 bytes, but changed 36 of the 5,400 certification actions . It failed the project’s exact action-parity criterion, so the FP32 model was retained. Changed actions are not automatically unsafe actions. The recorded experiment establishes a parity failure; it does not demonstrate that all 36 changes caused collisions. The practical lesson is to re-evaluate behavior after compression before promoting a new artifact. The GPU training record needs similar care. It reports a training duration of about 16.48 seconds on an RTX 3050 laptop GPU, but identifies a candidate that was rejected. That duration should not be advertised as the verified training time of the deployed checkpoint or the complete data-generation-and-training workflow.

title: Tiny Dino: A 21,699-Parameter Policy That Plays Without a Safety Net
heading: Keeping the evidence attached to the weights
text: One of the strongest engineering details is the checkpoint evidence chain. The runtime checks the checkpoint schema, engine revision, feature version, and feature-layout hash before loading the model. This reduces the risk of silently feeding weights a different interpretation of the inputs. An end-to-end test then ties the checkpoint’s SHA-256 hash to the certification, evidence summary, and soak records. Its purpose is straightforward: establish that the model being served is the model named in those records. A passing report for yesterday’s weights should not become evidence for today’s replacement file.

It shows how much a small network can do in a deliberately scoped environment—and how carefully the claim must follow the evidence.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Introduction
text: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google’s latest open embedding model for semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Built on Gemma 4, it maps text, source code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional vector space. It is released under the Apache 2.0 license and scales from 270 million to 740 million parameters depending on the modalities you enable.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Why EmbeddingGemma 2 matters?
text: Traditional multimodal search systems often require separate models for text, images, audio, and video. EmbeddingGemma 2 provides a unified alternative: Search source code using natural-language queries. Find images using text descriptions. Search audio recordings and video clips semantically. Build multimodal RAG pipelines. Run local or on-device retrieval with a relatively small model. Store embeddings in a single compatible vector space. For example, a query such as “waterproof trail shoes” can be compared with text, product images, or a video showing the shoes being tested on wet rocks.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Main Specifications
text: Feature Details Model EmbeddingGemma 2 Base model Gemma 4 License Apache 2.0 Modalities Text, code, images, video, and audio Maximum embedding size 768 dimensions Context window 8,192 tokens Parameter range 270M to 740M Embedding compression 768, 512, 256, or 128 dimensions Main use cases Semantic search, code search, multimodal retrieval, RAG, recommendation systems

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Modular architecture
text: You do not need to load the complete model if your application uses only one or two modalities. 270M parameters: Text and code. 440M parameters: Text, images, and video. 570M parameters: Text and audio. 740M parameters: Text, code, images, video, and audio. The different configurations still project inputs into the same vector space. This means a text-only encoder can be used with embeddings generated by the full multimodal configuration, provided the embedding dimensions and processing settings match.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Stronger code retrieval
text: One of the most useful improvements is its code-understanding capability. Google reports that EmbeddingGemma 2 performs 14% better than EmbeddingGemma 1 on the MTEB Code benchmark. This makes it suitable for: Searching large GitHub repositories. Finding relevant functions from natural-language questions. Building coding assistants. Indexing technical documentation and source code. Supporting agentic code-search workflows. A developer could ask: “Where is authentication token refresh implemented?” The embedding model can retrieve the most relevant files, classes, or functions before an LLM generates the final answer.

title: EmbeddingGemma 2: A Compact Multimodal Embedding Model
heading: Matryoshka Representation Learning
text: EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning, or MRL. This allows the original 768-dimensional vector to be truncated to a smaller size while preserving much of its semantic quality. Dimensions Recommended use 768 or 512 Highest recall and multimodal retrieval 256 Storage-constrained indexes 128 Large text-only indexes and first-stage shortlisting At 256 dimensions, the model retains most of its quality for text and code and approximately 95% of its retrieval quality for image, video, and speech. At 128 dimensions, text and code retain around 90% quality, while multimodal retrieval quality can fall to approximately 75%. These figures should be validated against your own data before deployment. Reducing the vector size can significantly lower storage requirements. For example, one million 768-dimensional vectors require roughly 1.5 GB in bfloat16, while 128-dimensional vectors require approximately 250 MB.

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: Introduction
text: Draft-verify-accept in ~60 lines of PyTorch, then HF assisted generation + llama.cpp — 2–3× faster inference, proven lossless.

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: What we covered
text: Autoregressive decoding is slow because it generates one token per forward pass. Speculative decoding breaks that bottleneck — with zero change in outputs. - Draft-verify-accept — a small draft model proposes tokens, the big model verifies them in parallel. Accept the matches, keep the guarantees. - Why it is lossless — the acceptance criterion provably preserves the target distribution. Speed without sampling drift. - HF assisted generation + llama.cpp — the same idea in production tooling, configured and benchmarked live.

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: What we built
text: A 60-line PyTorch draft-verify-accept loop, then assisted generation in Transformers and a llama.cpp run — speedups measured on the room's own machines, outputs verified identical.

title: Speculative Decoding — 2-3x Faster Inference in 60 Lines of PyTorch
heading: Takeaways
text: - The fastest token is the one you don't recompute — verification parallelizes, drafting is cheap. - Lossless matters: speculation is an exact optimization, not an approximation. - 64 people, one lab, every laptop showing the same speedup. That is the AIYatra format.
